title: ROBERT SCOTT CARPENTER: 'They were using the paddles and I was losing my mind'; Shooting kills dream life
article: Robert Scott Carpenter sings for his wife every day. He's been dead seven months now -- shot by an Amherstburg police officer -- but his rock 'n' roll voice still resonates on a tape he made for Lisa Stewart; the same way it did when she first saw him on stage, the same way it always will.
Curled up on the couch in her Harrow home or lying alone in bed, hazel eyes staring at the ceiling, the diminutive Stewart presses play on her Walkman and drifts back to better days.
"I listen to that tape every day and when the kids ask about him I throw on the tape and say 'That's Daddy, you can hear him,' " says Stewart.
"It helps. If I have to go out and do something and I don't feel strong enough, I put on that tape. I listen to it and I'm going to be fine."

Carpenter, 36, was shot and killed shortly after 7 a.m. Oct. 30 in the front foyer of the three-bedroom home he shared with Stewart, his common-law wife, at 258 McCurdy Dr. He was shot in the right femoral artery and collapsed on his front lawn as Stewart wailed beside him. He was pronounced dead three hours later at hospital.
Stewart, 28, relives those final agonizing minutes again and again.
Carpenter croaked for something to drink as he bled to death in front of his children. Stewart ran into the split-level house and poured orange Gatorade into a tea cup and rushed back outside.

She tipped a trickle into his mouth and realized he was shaking uncontrollably. Stewart ran inside again and grabbed three comforters. She placed a blanket underneath his legs and torso and draped another over his quivering body.
She pleaded for him to hang on -- promised that she'd be good, that she'd do anything if he could just hang on -- but her tears were in vain.
"He made eye contact with me and said I love you and then there was no pulse," she says.
"They were using the paddles and I was losing my mind."
As Stewart talks about the life she shared with Carpenter -- a life that revolved around music and their two children, Sarah, 4 and Noah, 3, -- she absently strokes a tattoo on her ring finger.

About a month after Carpenter died, Stewart paid $60 for a small blue and purple rendering of a flower. Carpenter, a Scorpio, had a scorpion tattooed on his ring finger and Stewart says she was going to get a matching tattoo -- she's an Aquarian -- when they got married.
She settled on a flower because Carpenter loved gardening; the backyard of their Amherstburg home boasted a lush garden and a pond and fountain that Carpenter fashioned himself.
On her other hand she wears a small gold and diamond ring Carpenter gave her when they started dating. "We promised each other that we would always be together," she says.
"We would have been together forever but somebody decided that wasn't meant to be."

Stewart was a cashier at the University of Windsor bookstore in January 1995 when she met Carpenter at a friend's house in Windsor. She watched as he talked a pair of drunks out of fighting each other and says she felt a "spark."
When she saw Carpenter singing in the band Nightbreed at the Canusa a few days later, it became a fire.
"He was the singer and I was just in awe. There's no words to describe it," she says.
"When I met him it was like a fairytale."
Life in those heady early days was like some fast and loose rock 'n' roll fantasy. Stewart had a roommate and Carpenter lived with his parents so the two would spend every night in a different hotel.

Like a band on the road, they'd lug around Carpenter's guitar, taking taxis everywhere and eating where they could, sleeping during the day and rocking in a different bar every night. Sometimes they'd just sit in the park and play guitar.
"It was like being famous," says Stewart.
Carpenter, a Centennial high school graduate, landed a job on the line at Chrysler shortly after meeting Stewart and the couple moved into an apartment on Meldrum Road.
He worked for about three years and then went on disability leave because of his sciatic nerve.
Carpenter slowly pulled back from the rock 'n' roll lifestyle -- he'd play with the band when he was working days but skip the gigs when he was working afternoons -- and became a family man.

Stewart gave birth to Sarah in December 1996 and shortly after became pregnant with Noah. In August 1997, when Sarah was eight months old and Stewart was five-months pregnant, the couple moved into their dream home on McCurdy Drive in the riverside town of Amherstburg.

They built a music studio in the basement -- Carpenter would play his guitar every day and had splurged on a Les Paul shortly before he died -- and fashioned a backyard paradise. Snapshots show a tropical garden and fountain surrounded by toys and playground equipment.
Stewart was a stay-at-home mom and Carpenter, still on disability insurance, was a stay-at-home dad.

Every Tuesday was new-release night at the local video store and they'd get a bag of popcorn and hunker down to watch movies with the kids. They rarely went to bars but they played cards, doted on the kids and walked along the riverfront with their miniature dobermans, Taffy and Spike.
The couple were early risers and would read the newspaper every morning. Carpenter was taking computer and journalism courses at St. Clair College and dreamed of writing for a newspaper.
"His idea was to have a good newspaper; a paper that was only filled with good news," says Stewart, shaking her head at the way he finally made the front page.

The final, tragic chapter in their love story began unfolding two weeks before Carpenter was killed, says Stewart. Her lover quit smoking and began acting paranoid. He believed he was going to die before his 37th birthday on Nov. 6.
When they were walking through a store, Carpenter asked Stewart if she had heard a shopper say "I'll see you on Halloween." She hadn't.
"It just came out of the blue. He kept to himself. He did a lot of writing. He was just different; he was just very, very quiet," says Stewart.
"He said we were in danger until Halloween but I brushed it off because I didn't know what he meant. I thought it was a mid-life crisis."

Stewart couldn't understand the "bizarre" changes in Carpenter and now believes he had a premonition of his death. She says he wasn't a drug user, adding a toxicology report commissioned after the shooting indicates Carpenter only had trace amounts of Ibuprofen in his system.

But his behaviour was out of character. Carpenter was easygoing, says Stewart; he never yelled or raised his hand to the children. And he would go out of his way to help people. He wouldn't just give money to panhandlers, he would buy them a meal or coffee.
Stewart says he wasn't suicidal and points out they bought new furniture and, just 19 days before Carpenter was killed, a used Grand Cherokee limited-edition jeep for $7,000.
The couple spent the night before the shooting buying Halloween candy -- Sarah was supposed to be a princess last year and Noah was going to be a pumpkin -- and never went to bed.

Carpenter's behaviour turned more erratic as night turned to morning and, at one point, says Stewart, he waved a crowbar around and yelled through the living room window at his imaginary foes outside to come and take him on.
"I asked him if somebody had dropped something on him. He wasn't himself. He hadn't been himself for nearly two weeks," she says.
Stewart became so alarmed that she phoned 911. She hung up mid- call but it was too late.
Carpenter's bloody premonition was about to play itself out in front of Stewart and their two children.
"I feel I betrayed him," says Stewart.
"My life was pretty much blown to pieces that day."

Memories of the shooting kept her away from her McCurdy Drive home and the rumours swirling in the coffee shops of Amherstburg drove her out of the community. The gossip stemming from the shooting forced her to pack her bags for Harrow.
It hasn't been easy -- she receives death benefits of $540 a month but it barely covers her rent -- and she doesn't think the inquest into the shooting will make it any easier.
"I don't think it's going to help me. It's not going to change what happened. Nothing can change that," she says, adding she needs to hear that the officer who shot her husband is truly sorry.
